end of university so I was doing law and well I was on course for a first and I was just coming
up to my my final exams and I had a few essays and a few exams and so I just started working
really hard.
I felt like right now was the real time to put the effort in and to put the work in. So I started to
step a bit later and take on a bit more work so my stress levels sort of started to increase over a
while. I was drinking a lot more coffee, took a few caffeine tablets and energy drinks.
A few people well because sort of the environment at the time was a lot of people were pushing
themselves that they wouldn't normally do and some people were taking Ritalin. Did you take
any Ritalin? Yeah because it was just like it was that was necessary at the time. How did that
affect you? Well it sort of increased my confidence at the time, everything that was going on.
I was becoming a lot more productive, a lot more confident, I was working harder, my brain
was working faster and so my momentum was building up and up throughout the period. So I
was relishing it and I was doing a lot of work. So what did that mean to you then to be at that
time? It sounds like you put quite a lot of pressure on yourself, you've been doing really well at
uni and you know this was it, this was the time.
What did it mean to you to be feeling like that kind of more awake and more energised maybe?
Yeah well for me it was it was my sort of time. So I'd spent three years, I was in control, I was
doing well. It wasn't really part of my life at the time, I didn't really talk to any of my friends
about it but then I started to just sort of grow into it and I took the opportunity to enjoy this
time and it didn't really reach its peak until after my exams.
I was still functioning throughout my exams. I have since found out that I didn't get the results
that I wanted to Why do you think that was? Well I thought that I was working harder than ever
but it was misjudged I think and so I didn't perform to the best of my ability when it came to the
exams and so I didn't achieve a first time and only got two on. What else was happening for you
around that time? I mean you talked about the pressure of your exams and staying up for
them, was anything else going on for you around the same time? Well so it was the end of the
end of university and that was the time where well as soon as that period stopped of work then

I was sort of let off the leash a bit and yeah I just thought to grow even further.
So I mentioned I was taking Ritalin, drinking a lot of coffee and as soon as my exams had
stopped I just substance abuse sort of took a bit more of a hold and yeah I just sort of grew into
this person who I thought was him, was the guy that everyone wanted to be around and to see
and so I made sure that I was just everywhere to be seen. So this is like the gap after you finish
the exams but before the results are out? Yeah, so we were just going out a lot but if not every
night. You said that you were taking Ritalin and drinking a lot of coffee and using other drugs
as well? Yeah sort of developed into cocaine a lot, MDMA, MCAT.
And how did they affect you? I honestly was on cloud nine at the time and yeah I was just, I was
the person that everyone wanted to know in my head. I put myself at the centre of the universe
and I even, I convinced a friend of mine who develops apps that we should, I had an idea to
develop an app about when you go into a alcohol shop that it all weigh up, like what's the most
cost effective way to get wasted. So yeah I mean at the time I was spending a lot of money, a lot
of my parents' savings.
I'd got a credit card which I didn't tell them about and so in this sort of role as the man, as the
man about town I was spent a lot on alcohol, drugs, clothes, I invested in this technology and
yeah I was... So it sounds like it began with kind of the exam pressure and putting more
pressure on yourself to stay up, using kind of stimulants to keep yourself awake and then you
started to feel like you were more and more the man, you were kind of popular, you were
successful. How did you respond and cope with those symptoms? What did you do once those
are kind of begun? Well having not had to deal with my illness throughout university and for it
not being a part of that world, I didn't confront those symptoms in a way that's going to have
long-term sort of stability. It began with doing the work that I needed to do, that's just what I
needed to do in order to achieve my goals and to achieve what I want to and then I just let it
take hold and it was all part of it.
It wasn't the illness, it was me. I was the master of this whole situation and everything that was
happening was down to my own doing. So it sounds, you say on the one hand you didn't
confront it, you kind of just let it roll and on the other hand you said that you kind of took it as
evidence that you were very energetic, you were powerful, this was all kind of explained about
who you were and I guess how did that affect you looking at things in that way? It just, it was
my time.
It had all been leading to this was the moment where I would sort of become the person that I
wanted to be. All the hard work, all everything, like all the work that my parents had done for
me, all the work that I'd been doing, it was now crystallising. It felt like you were on the brink of
something enormous from the sounds of it.
Again going back to that kind of beginning stage where you started to stay up late and use
stimulants, I mean how much sleep were you getting at the beginning? It gradually diminished
I think. It began at six, five and then was ended up about three and two hours. What kind of

things did you notice? Did you notice any changes from having less and less sleep in your body
maybe or the way you were thinking? I think the harder I was working, the faster my brain then
would work and how much, the harder I worked, the more I would do.
So it wasn't, it was just the momentum was building more than anything. My thoughts were
firing and my goals were stronger and my determination was bigger. And how did you feel in
your body? Did you notice any changes physically? Not that I can recall.
At the time maybe I was trying to, maybe I was avoiding confronting any negative effects but
nothing powerful comes to mind. Okay. And once things were a bit further along after your
exams, you said you were going out a lot, you convinced your friend to do this app.
Was there anything else that you did that maybe you wouldn't normally do that you think
might've been a sign to you that your mood was much higher than you'd like it to be? I had a lot
of savings that my parents had built up for me, which don't really exist anymore. Either through
the money I invested and through drugs, clothes. I had a girlfriend at the time but because it
was, because I was the main character in a sense that I was only the person that mattered.
And so those around me, especially her, didn't really have as much importance. So on nights
out, she just wouldn't be in my mind and so there would be other women. Okay.
And how do you feel about that now, looking back on it? I think it's those moments where it's
not just me, it's those closest to you and those around you that have to suffer more than
anyone else. That brings a lot of the shame.

a few questions I wanted to speak to the consultant about.
I'm the registrar who's looking after your father at the moment. The consultant's not here, I can
try and answer some of your questions if that's alright with you. Yeah, if you can help that,
that's great, yeah.
Yeah, that's fine. Before we start, I just want to confirm you've had permission from your father
for me to talk to you about all of this today, is that right? Yeah, I'm his next of kin, so he's given
me full permission to talk to you. He's obviously not really well enough at the moment to hold a
conversation, so he's confident that it's best that I take the information in and feed it back to
him.
Okay. And how much do you know about your father's condition and where we're up to with
him at the moment? Well, obviously, he's got cancer, I know that, and he's very ill, he's very
uncomfortable, very poorly, and I suppose we're all, the family, we're quite aware that it's just a
matter of time, really. Yeah.
Okay. And are you aware about our plans for what we will do if he gets more poorly? You mean
the... The do not resuscitate? Yeah, yeah, yeah, we're aware of that. You're aware of that, and
you're happy that that's in place? Yes, that's what my father wants, and I think that's the best
thing for him.
And, so yes, he has got cancer, and he's very poorly at the moment, as you can see and as
you've said, and I think we're, after seeing the deterioration that's happened in him since he's
been admitted, we can see that he's, unfortunately, nearing the end of his life now. Yeah. I just
wanted to see if there's anything that can be done to sort of manage his pain a bit more.
He just seems really agitated, and I'm just finding it really difficult to see him in this state at the
moment. And that's normal. Okay.
It's not, it's never nice seeing a loved one in this sort of a situation. Okay. And from our point of
view going forward now, our focus needs to be on what we can do to keep him as comfortable
as possible, as opposed to actually actively treating him.
Okay. So we're not trying to treat his cancer or treat any of his conditions, we're trying to deal
with the symptoms and make him as comfortable as possible. Okay.

So, you mentioned the pain. Yeah. So at the moment he's on a morphine patch, all right, and it's
important now that we're sort of switching to a palliative approach, that we look at that in more
detail.
Because if we're not controlling his pain, there's lots more things we can add in. All right. Given
that his level of consciousness isn't good, I don't want us to be doing that in tablet form,
obviously.
I don't think he would be in a situation where swallowing tablets and things like that are going

medication through a syringe driver.
Like a needle. So essentially it's a needle that just sits under the skin, and it's attached to a
syringe that's got a make-up of medications in that it's constantly going to be giving him. Okay.
To give him a good amount of pain relief. So it stays there all the time. Yeah.
So he'll be attached to it. Also, I'll make sure we prescribe some more as-required medication,
so that if that syringe driver's not giving him enough, the nurses have the ability to recognise
that and give him a top-up. Okay.
Well, I've been aware that he's quite uncomfortable. And I know he's not had a bowel

moment, and if there's anything we can possibly do about that just to make him more
comfortable. Yeah.
From a bowel sort of perspective, it's slightly difficult in that if we're worried about his

don't want us to be pushing too hard with tablets and things like that, because I don't think his
swallow's safe to be doing that at the moment. No.
All right. Equally, if he's in pain, then I think really the thing to do is to give him more morphine

Also, you mentioned that he's quite distressed and agitated. Yeah. So we have some other

All right? That should help to keep him calm, all right? And help to deal with the distress that

Okay. But, what I would much rather you do is let people know and give them the opportunity

So how aware is he? I've not had a chance to speak to him yet. So at this moment in time, he

to you about any wishes that he would want in a situation where he's unable to express his own
wishes. But nonetheless, we don't think he's in pain or in any distress at the moment.
Well, that's good to know. Yeah, and we will be assessing. We see him daily on the ward rounds,

independent person.

Okay. So I'm not quite sure what you're alluding to. Sure.

And what's your experience of that? Well, I don't know much around it, but I know that she was

life. But that's not always the most appropriate thing to do.

best interest of this person. So normally we would have these conversations with someone
who's able to engage in the conversations and tell us their prior wishes.
But whilst dad is not able to do that, we have these conversations with the relatives and the

So with all these conversations there, they're very difficult and the decisions are very difficult.

electric shocks across the chest in order to restart a heart that has already stopped. If the

unlikely to be successful and may cause harm, including rib fractures, punctured lungs and
brain injury. When the heart stops in these cases, resuscitation does not prevent death and will
prolong suffering.

prognosis, it is likely that their heart stopping will be the end stage of a natural dying process
and therefore attempts at resuscitation will not be in their interest. It is important that the
candidate explains that resuscitation decisions are primarily a medical decision made to
prevent harm and suffering. In this case, the patient does not have capacity, which is why this
discussion is being had with the family member.
The candidate should ensure that the family member understands what they're explaining
throughout, answer any questions and is sensitive to their concerns and views at all times. They

should understand that this can be a distressing conversation and that the family members
may require time to digest all the information that is being given.

tests.description:
Ground Truth reference: Nice to see you again Tom, how are you today? I'm okay. So I understand that since I was
seeing you that while ago that you're in hospital again. Yeah.
So can you tell me a bit more about what happened before that? Well it was a few months ago
now, yeah I'd done quite well for a number of years sort of kept it under control really. Yeah I
mean I've not seen you since your gap year wasn't it? Yeah so that was four years ago. So yeah
it was quite disappointing to to go through it all again but it sort of started at the towards the
end of university so I was doing law and well I was on course for a first and I was just coming
up to my my final exams and I had a few essays and a few exams and so I just started working
really hard.
I felt like right now was the real time to put the effort in and to put the work in. So I started to
step a bit later and take on a bit more work so my stress levels sort of started to increase over a
while. I was drinking a lot more coffee, took a few caffeine tablets and energy drinks.
A few people well because sort of the environment at the time was a lot of people were pushing
themselves that they wouldn't normally do and some people were taking Ritalin. Did you take
any Ritalin? Yeah because it was just like it was that was necessary at the time. How did that
affect you? Well it sort of increased my confidence at the time, everything that was going on.
I was becoming a lot more productive, a lot more confident, I was working harder, my brain
was working faster and so my momentum was building up and up throughout the period. So I
was relishing it and I was doing a lot of work. So what did that mean to you then to be at that
time? It sounds like you put quite a lot of pressure on yourself, you've been doing really well at
uni and you know this was it, this was the time.
What did it mean to you to be feeling like that kind of more awake and more energised maybe?
Yeah well for me it was it was my sort of time. So I'd spent three years, I was in control, I was
doing well. It wasn't really part of my life at the time, I didn't really talk to any of my friends
about it but then I started to just sort of grow into it and I took the opportunity to enjoy this
time and it didn't really reach its peak until after my exams.
I was still functioning throughout my exams. I have since found out that I didn't get the results
that I wanted to Why do you think that was? Well I thought that I was working harder than ever
but it was misjudged I think and so I didn't perform to the best of my ability when it came to the
exams and so I didn't achieve a first time and only got two on. What else was happening for you
around that time? I mean you talked about the pressure of your exams and staying up for
them, was anything else going on for you around the same time? Well so it was the end of the
end of university and that was the time where well as soon as that period stopped of work then

I was sort of let off the leash a bit and yeah I just thought to grow even further.
So I mentioned I was taking Ritalin, drinking a lot of coffee and as soon as my exams had
stopped I just substance abuse sort of took a bit more of a hold and yeah I just sort of grew into
this person who I thought was him, was the guy that everyone wanted to be around and to see
and so I made sure that I was just everywhere to be seen. So this is like the gap after you finish
the exams but before the results are out? Yeah, so we were just going out a lot but if not every
night. You said that you were taking Ritalin and drinking a lot of coffee and using other drugs
as well? Yeah sort of developed into cocaine a lot, MDMA, MCAT.
And how did they affect you? I honestly was on cloud nine at the time and yeah I was just, I was
the person that everyone wanted to know in my head. I put myself at the centre of the universe
and I even, I convinced a friend of mine who develops apps that we should, I had an idea to
develop an app about when you go into a alcohol shop that it all weigh up, like what's the most
cost effective way to get wasted. So yeah I mean at the time I was spending a lot of money, a lot
of my parents' savings.
I'd got a credit card which I didn't tell them about and so in this sort of role as the man, as the
man about town I was spent a lot on alcohol, drugs, clothes, I invested in this technology and
yeah I was... So it sounds like it began with kind of the exam pressure and putting more
pressure on yourself to stay up, using kind of stimulants to keep yourself awake and then you
started to feel like you were more and more the man, you were kind of popular, you were
successful. How did you respond and cope with those symptoms? What did you do once those
are kind of begun? Well having not had to deal with my illness throughout university and for it
not being a part of that world, I didn't confront those symptoms in a way that's going to have
long-term sort of stability. It began with doing the work that I needed to do, that's just what I
needed to do in order to achieve my goals and to achieve what I want to and then I just let it
take hold and it was all part of it.
It wasn't the illness, it was me. I was the master of this whole situation and everything that was
happening was down to my own doing. So it sounds, you say on the one hand you didn't
confront it, you kind of just let it roll and on the other hand you said that you kind of took it as
evidence that you were very energetic, you were powerful, this was all kind of explained about
who you were and I guess how did that affect you looking at things in that way? It just, it was
my time.
It had all been leading to this was the moment where I would sort of become the person that I
wanted to be. All the hard work, all everything, like all the work that my parents had done for
me, all the work that I'd been doing, it was now crystallising. It felt like you were on the brink of
something enormous from the sounds of it.
Again going back to that kind of beginning stage where you started to stay up late and use
stimulants, I mean how much sleep were you getting at the beginning? It gradually diminished
I think. It began at six, five and then was ended up about three and two hours. What kind of

things did you notice? Did you notice any changes from having less and less sleep in your body
maybe or the way you were thinking? I think the harder I was working, the faster my brain then
would work and how much, the harder I worked, the more I would do.
So it wasn't, it was just the momentum was building more than anything. My thoughts were
firing and my goals were stronger and my determination was bigger. And how did you feel in
your body? Did you notice any changes physically? Not that I can recall.
At the time maybe I was trying to, maybe I was avoiding confronting any negative effects but
nothing powerful comes to mind. Okay. And once things were a bit further along after your
exams, you said you were going out a lot, you convinced your friend to do this app.
Was there anything else that you did that maybe you wouldn't normally do that you think
might've been a sign to you that your mood was much higher than you'd like it to be? I had a lot
of savings that my parents had built up for me, which don't really exist anymore. Either through
the money I invested and through drugs, clothes. I had a girlfriend at the time but because it
was, because I was the main character in a sense that I was only the person that mattered.
And so those around me, especially her, didn't really have as much importance. So on nights
out, she just wouldn't be in my mind and so there would be other women. Okay.
And how do you feel about that now, looking back on it? I think it's those moments where it's
not just me, it's those closest to you and those around you that have to suffer more than
anyone else. That brings a lot of the shame.

Addressing the emotions and offering an empathetic response.

uncertain. Before discussing a treatment plan, it is important to ask patients if they are ready at

ward, is that right? Yeah, well this is the first opportunity I've had to get here and be able to

Okay, well, you know, thank you for coming in. And what I hope to do today is talk you through

significant amount of weakness on that side. And because of the extent of the stroke, it's
affecting some of the functions that the brain would normally help with. So for example, his

a tube in his nose going into his stomach.
And then also having the physiotherapy team to see him on a daily basis to try and strengthen

independent person.
To think that that's potentially been taken away from him, I don't know that he will manage not
having that same amount of independence anymore. Yeah, of course. I mean, you've seen him
as an independent person, and now he's obviously very dependent on us for medications, for

Okay. So I'm not quite sure what you're alluding to. Sure.

And what's your experience of that? Well, I don't know much around it, but I know that she was

what treatments would be appropriate at that point? And sometimes we can offer things like
electric shocks to the heart or compressions to the chest to try and bring that person back to
life. But that's not always the most appropriate thing to do.
And sometimes allowing a natural death and a more dignified death is more appropriate. I

And what sort of, what's driving that? What are you thinking at the moment? I don't know. I

I think, you know, you've seen him so independent as you said, it can be very, very difficult to

is a decision that we make as a medical team and we try to think about what is likely to be in the
best interest of this person. So normally we would have these conversations with someone
who's able to engage in the conversations and tell us their prior wishes.
But whilst dad is not able to do that, we have these conversations with the relatives and the
next of kin. Now, because of the extent of the stroke and the fact that this is now not reversible,
we feel that if dad were to get to the point such that his heart stopped beating or he stopped
breathing, then that would likely represent the end of a natural dying process for him.

electric shocks, would not prevent death and would potentially cause more harm through rib
fractures or further brain damage.
And that would impair quality of life even further. I appreciate what you're saying. Is it possible

So with all these conversations there, they're very difficult and the decisions are very difficult.

need to hear from somebody else what you're telling me as well.
Yeah, no, of course. I completely understand that and we can arrange that for you. I think what
I would like to kind of emphasise here is that this discussion and this decision, it only refers to
the event of what we call a cardiac arrest or a respiratory arrest, i.e. the heart stops beating or
he stops breathing.
It doesn't impact the care that we currently give him. So we will continue to ensure that he has
his physiotherapy, that he gets the medications he needs to treat the stroke, that he gets
nutrition, fluids, any potential antibiotics or oxygen that he might need. So all those things we

acknowledge these and attempt to address them by providing reassurance and explanations.

way to begin discussions surrounding resuscitation.

negatively impact on other aspects of their father's care, for example, provision of antibiotics,
fluids, analgesia and other treatments required to prevent deterioration.
A good candidate will explain that resuscitation involves chest compressions and delivering
electric shocks across the chest in order to restart a heart that has already stopped. If the
reason the patient heart has stopped is the end result of a natural dying process, then this is
unlikely to be successful and may cause harm, including rib fractures, punctured lungs and
brain injury. When the heart stops in these cases, resuscitation does not prevent death and will
prolong suffering.
In the case of this patient, if they were to become more unwell, given their comorbidities and
prognosis, it is likely that their heart stopping will be the end stage of a natural dying process
and therefore attempts at resuscitation will not be in their interest. It is important that the
candidate explains that resuscitation decisions are primarily a medical decision made to
prevent harm and suffering. In this case, the patient does not have capacity, which is why this
discussion is being had with the family member.
The candidate should ensure that the family member understands what they're explaining
throughout, answer any questions and is sensitive to their concerns and views at all times. They

should understand that this can be a distressing conversation and that the family members
may require time to digest all the information that is being given.

tests.moduleLabel: Core System (Health, Auth, Audio Formats, Language)

tests.moduleLabel: Core System (Health, Auth, Audio Formats, Language)
tests.title: Tests JWT token minting via POST /auth/token using valid API key credentials. Validates that the authentication microservice signs and returns a secure, time-bounded bearer token with valid expiration timestamps, allowing subsequent authorized access to all STT and TTS API endpoints.

tests.moduleLabel: Core System (Health, Auth, Audio Formats, Language)
tests.title: Security negative test verifying that POST /auth/token strictly rejects malformed, invalid, or unauthorized API keys with HTTP 401 Unauthorized or HTTP 400 Bad Request, ensuring zero unauthorized access to downstream speech-to-text and voice synthesis compute resources.

tests.moduleLabel: Core System (Health, Auth, Audio Formats, Language)
tests.title: Validates 16kHz uncompressed PCM WAV audio decoding and end-to-end transcription pipeline via POST /v1/audio/transcriptions. Asserts non-empty text generation, accurate word timestamp segmentation, correct sample rate parsing, and robust audio header ingestion.

tests.title: Tests compressed MPEG Layer-3 (MP3) audio ingestion and decoding across variable bitrates. Asserts that the backend audio pre-processor unpacks MP3 frames accurately, normalizes audio streams, and executes speech-to-text inference without loss of linguistic fidelity.

Ground Truth reference: Nice to see you again Tom, how are you today? I'm okay. So I understand that since I was
seeing you that while ago that you're in hospital again. Yeah.
So can you tell me a bit more about what happened before that? Well it was a few months ago
now, yeah I'd done quite well for a number of years sort of kept it under control really. Yeah I
mean I've not seen you since your gap year wasn't it? Yeah so that was four years ago. So yeah
it was quite disappointing to to go through it all again but it sort of started at the towards the
end of university so I was doing law and well I was on course for a first and I was just coming
up to my my final exams and I had a few essays and a few exams and so I just started working
really hard.
I felt like right now was the real time to put the effort in and to put the work in. So I started to
step a bit later and take on a bit more work so my stress levels sort of started to increase over a
while. I was drinking a lot more coffee, took a few caffeine tablets and energy drinks.
A few people well because sort of the environment at the time was a lot of people were pushing
themselves that they wouldn't normally do and some people were taking Ritalin. Did you take
any Ritalin? Yeah because it was just like it was that was necessary at the time. How did that
affect you? Well it sort of increased my confidence at the time, everything that was going on.
I was becoming a lot more productive, a lot more confident, I was working harder, my brain
was working faster and so my momentum was building up and up throughout the period. So I
was relishing it and I was doing a lot of work. So what did that mean to you then to be at that
time? It sounds like you put quite a lot of pressure on yourself, you've been doing really well at
uni and you know this was it, this was the time.
What did it mean to you to be feeling like that kind of more awake and more energised maybe?
Yeah well for me it was it was my sort of time. So I'd spent three years, I was in control, I was
doing well. It wasn't really part of my life at the time, I didn't really talk to any of my friends
about it but then I started to just sort of grow into it and I took the opportunity to enjoy this
time and it didn't really reach its peak until after my exams.
I was still functioning throughout my exams. I have since found out that I didn't get the results
that I wanted to Why do you think that was? Well I thought that I was working harder than ever
but it was misjudged I think and so I didn't perform to the best of my ability when it came to the
exams and so I didn't achieve a first time and only got two on. What else was happening for you
around that time? I mean you talked about the pressure of your exams and staying up for
them, was anything else going on for you around the same time? Well so it was the end of the
end of university and that was the time where well as soon as that period stopped of work then

I was sort of let off the leash a bit and yeah I just thought to grow even further.
So I mentioned I was taking Ritalin, drinking a lot of coffee and as soon as my exams had
stopped I just substance abuse sort of took a bit more of a hold and yeah I just sort of grew into
this person who I thought was him, was the guy that everyone wanted to be around and to see
and so I made sure that I was just everywhere to be seen. So this is like the gap after you finish
the exams but before the results are out? Yeah, so we were just going out a lot but if not every
night. You said that you were taking Ritalin and drinking a lot of coffee and using other drugs
as well? Yeah sort of developed into cocaine a lot, MDMA, MCAT.
And how did they affect you? I honestly was on cloud nine at the time and yeah I was just, I was
the person that everyone wanted to know in my head. I put myself at the centre of the universe
and I even, I convinced a friend of mine who develops apps that we should, I had an idea to
develop an app about when you go into a alcohol shop that it all weigh up, like what's the most
cost effective way to get wasted. So yeah I mean at the time I was spending a lot of money, a lot
of my parents' savings.
I'd got a credit card which I didn't tell them about and so in this sort of role as the man, as the
man about town I was spent a lot on alcohol, drugs, clothes, I invested in this technology and
yeah I was... So it sounds like it began with kind of the exam pressure and putting more
pressure on yourself to stay up, using kind of stimulants to keep yourself awake and then you
started to feel like you were more and more the man, you were kind of popular, you were
successful. How did you respond and cope with those symptoms? What did you do once those
are kind of begun? Well having not had to deal with my illness throughout university and for it
not being a part of that world, I didn't confront those symptoms in a way that's going to have
long-term sort of stability. It began with doing the work that I needed to do, that's just what I
needed to do in order to achieve my goals and to achieve what I want to and then I just let it
take hold and it was all part of it.
It wasn't the illness, it was me. I was the master of this whole situation and everything that was
happening was down to my own doing. So it sounds, you say on the one hand you didn't
confront it, you kind of just let it roll and on the other hand you said that you kind of took it as
evidence that you were very energetic, you were powerful, this was all kind of explained about
who you were and I guess how did that affect you looking at things in that way? It just, it was
my time.
It had all been leading to this was the moment where I would sort of become the person that I
wanted to be. All the hard work, all everything, like all the work that my parents had done for
me, all the work that I'd been doing, it was now crystallising. It felt like you were on the brink of
something enormous from the sounds of it.
Again going back to that kind of beginning stage where you started to stay up late and use
stimulants, I mean how much sleep were you getting at the beginning? It gradually diminished
I think. It began at six, five and then was ended up about three and two hours. What kind of

things did you notice? Did you notice any changes from having less and less sleep in your body
maybe or the way you were thinking? I think the harder I was working, the faster my brain then
would work and how much, the harder I worked, the more I would do.
So it wasn't, it was just the momentum was building more than anything. My thoughts were
firing and my goals were stronger and my determination was bigger. And how did you feel in
your body? Did you notice any changes physically? Not that I can recall.
At the time maybe I was trying to, maybe I was avoiding confronting any negative effects but
nothing powerful comes to mind. Okay. And once things were a bit further along after your
exams, you said you were going out a lot, you convinced your friend to do this app.
Was there anything else that you did that maybe you wouldn't normally do that you think
might've been a sign to you that your mood was much higher than you'd like it to be? I had a lot
of savings that my parents had built up for me, which don't really exist anymore. Either through
the money I invested and through drugs, clothes. I had a girlfriend at the time but because it
was, because I was the main character in a sense that I was only the person that mattered.
And so those around me, especially her, didn't really have as much importance. So on nights
out, she just wouldn't be in my mind and so there would be other women. Okay.
And how do you feel about that now, looking back on it? I think it's those moments where it's
not just me, it's those closest to you and those around you that have to suffer more than
anyone else. That brings a lot of the shame.

Ground Truth reference: Good afternoon. Afternoon. My name's Dr Farrant.
Are you Mr William's daughter, is that right? I am, yeah. Okay. And I believe you wanted to

a few questions I wanted to speak to the consultant about.
I'm the registrar who's looking after your father at the moment. The consultant's not here, I can
try and answer some of your questions if that's alright with you. Yeah, if you can help that,
that's great, yeah.
Yeah, that's fine. Before we start, I just want to confirm you've had permission from your father
for me to talk to you about all of this today, is that right? Yeah, I'm his next of kin, so he's given
me full permission to talk to you. He's obviously not really well enough at the moment to hold a
conversation, so he's confident that it's best that I take the information in and feed it back to
him.
Okay. And how much do you know about your father's condition and where we're up to with
him at the moment? Well, obviously, he's got cancer, I know that, and he's very ill, he's very
uncomfortable, very poorly, and I suppose we're all, the family, we're quite aware that it's just a
matter of time, really. Yeah.
Okay. And are you aware about our plans for what we will do if he gets more poorly? You mean
the... The do not resuscitate? Yeah, yeah, yeah, we're aware of that. You're aware of that, and
you're happy that that's in place? Yes, that's what my father wants, and I think that's the best
thing for him.
And, so yes, he has got cancer, and he's very poorly at the moment, as you can see and as
you've said, and I think we're, after seeing the deterioration that's happened in him since he's
been admitted, we can see that he's, unfortunately, nearing the end of his life now. Yeah. I just
wanted to see if there's anything that can be done to sort of manage his pain a bit more.
He just seems really agitated, and I'm just finding it really difficult to see him in this state at the
moment. And that's normal. Okay.
It's not, it's never nice seeing a loved one in this sort of a situation. Okay. And from our point of
view going forward now, our focus needs to be on what we can do to keep him as comfortable
as possible, as opposed to actually actively treating him.
Okay. So we're not trying to treat his cancer or treat any of his conditions, we're trying to deal
with the symptoms and make him as comfortable as possible. Okay.

So, you mentioned the pain. Yeah. So at the moment he's on a morphine patch, all right, and it's
important now that we're sort of switching to a palliative approach, that we look at that in more
detail.
Because if we're not controlling his pain, there's lots more things we can add in. All right. Given
that his level of consciousness isn't good, I don't want us to be doing that in tablet form,
obviously.
I don't think he would be in a situation where swallowing tablets and things like that are going
to be appropriate for him. Okay. So we'll be thinking about things like an infusion of pain
medication through a syringe driver.
Like a needle. So essentially it's a needle that just sits under the skin, and it's attached to a
syringe that's got a make-up of medications in that it's constantly going to be giving him. Okay.
To give him a good amount of pain relief. So it stays there all the time. Yeah.
So he'll be attached to it. Also, I'll make sure we prescribe some more as-required medication,
so that if that syringe driver's not giving him enough, the nurses have the ability to recognise
that and give him a top-up. Okay.
Well, I've been aware that he's quite uncomfortable. And I know he's not had a bowel
movement for a while now, and I'm just wondering if this is adding to his discomfort at the
moment, and if there's anything we can possibly do about that just to make him more
comfortable. Yeah.
From a bowel sort of perspective, it's slightly difficult in that if we're worried about his
swallowing, giving him things by mouth is a bit more difficult. So what we can do is we can use
things like enemas to try and help clear things out from the back passage perspective, but I
don't want us to be pushing too hard with tablets and things like that, because I don't think his
swallow's safe to be doing that at the moment. No.
All right. Equally, if he's in pain, then I think really the thing to do is to give him more morphine
and try and control his pain better from that to try and give him a bit more comfort. Okay.
Also, you mentioned that he's quite distressed and agitated. Yeah. So we have some other
medication that we can add into the syringe driver called midazolam to try and deal with his
agitation at this difficult time.
All right? That should help to keep him calm, all right? And help to deal with the distress that
he's clearly in at the moment. All right? Also, we'll be keeping an eye on him for other problems,
like if he starts getting difficulty with his breathing, we can give him some more morphine type
medication. If he's having lots of secretions, we've got medication to dampen that down.
We've also got medication we can give to deal with any sickness that he might be dealing with.

Okay? If he becomes more breathless from the mesothelioma, then we can give him some
oxygen just for a bit of comfort as well. Okay? Okay.
One thing that people normally ask in this situation is, how long are we looking at? Yeah, I did
want to bring that up, obviously. We have family up and down the country who obviously would
like to come in and see Dad. I don't know if it's possible for him to have some visitors over the
next few days.
Do we even have that much time? I don't know. So, I've been right lots of times and I've been
wrong lots of times. And so, I never like giving a cast iron guarantee on how long we have left
because it doesn't work like that.
Okay. But, what I would much rather you do is let people know and give them the opportunity
to come than us say, it'll take a week or we've got a week left. We may not.
So, I would suggest, now that he's quite poorly, letting people know and giving people the
opportunity to make their own decision and come down if they need to and they feel that that's
something they would want to do. Okay. And, just in terms of, again, just trying to make things
a little bit easier for him, I was just wondering, you know, obviously he's not really able to eat
very much but can I perhaps bring him something homemade, some homemade soup,
something like that? Would that be possible? So, if he sort of regains consciousness to the point
where he can eat, then I have no problem with him having some home comfort.
But, equally, he is very poorly at the moment. Alright. And, I don't want us to be giving him
things if his swallowing is not safe and his conscious level is not good enough for that because
that could make him more distressed.
I don't want him to aspirate and soup things to go into his lungs because that wouldn't be very
good for him. So, I think we just need to see how he gets on over the next 24 hours or so. If he
gets a little bit better, then that's something we could look at.
I know. I also wanted to ask, a few days ago, obviously he's got this fracture in his spine as well
that he's having to cope with. The nurses managed to sit him up a little bit.
And, when he was sat up, he seemed to have, I don't know, just a little bit more brightness
about him. I mean, I was just wondering, is there any way we can do that without obviously
causing him any pain? But, it just gave him a kind of something, a bit of something, you know.
Okay.
So, yes, I think we can sit him up. Now that we're in a sort of a palliative situation and we think
he's nearing the end of his life, it's less of a concern about the risks to his spinal cord and things
like that from sitting him up with this back fracture. But, I don't want us to just sit him up too
much.
So, I think we should do it gradually and see how his pain responds to that. Okay. Okay.

So, just to summarise, obviously he does very poorly. We're switching his sort of treatment aims
now to an end-of-life treatment plan. We'll be treating his symptoms and not his underlying
condition.
Okay. And, I think it's a good idea now that if there are family members you want to give a call
and ask them to come and see him, now would be the time to do so. Thank you.
Thank you. The ICE and SPICES models are well-recognised frameworks that can be used by
candidates in communication skills and it can help you frame your discussion for breaking bad
news. SPICES can be split up into Step 1, Setting.
Make sure that you're in a private setting and invite the daughter to bring along someone for
support. Before meeting with the relative, you will have already confirmed that you will have
the patient's consent to discuss their case with the relative. Step 2, Perception.
Use the before-you-tell, ask strategy of starting with an open-ended question, such as, thank
you for meeting with me today, my name is Dr X. So, we are meeting today to discuss how to
best manage your father's condition and in particular his pain control relating to his cancer. But
I just want to start by establishing what you understand about his condition presently. The
response to this open-ended question will allow you to determine how much the relative
understands and at the same time offer the relative the opportunity to pose questions to you.
Step 3, Invite the relative to express how much they wish to know. Examples of questions asked
to the patient would be, sometimes patients and relatives want to go into detail about the
management of their care and other people would prefer to focus on the specific points. Before
I start, I just wanted to establish what you wanted to discuss and how much detail you would
like me to go into.
Step 4, Giving knowledge. Unfortunately, I've got some bad news to tell you or I'm sorry to tell
you that. I'll just run through four important points to consider.
Point 1, pitch the discussion at the level of comprehension for the daughter. Point 2, make sure
that you use non-technical information. Point 3, give the information in bite-sized chunks rather
than all at once.
Point 4, periodically check the person's understanding. At this point, it would be appropriate to
discuss specific end-of-life issues. Introduce this by saying something along the lines of, when
patients have terminal cancer and are nearing the end of life, there are specific targets for
treatment that we try to address preemptively.
To counteract pain, we prescribe medications that sometimes contain morphine. If the patient
is unable to take this by mouth, then we can give this by injection or sometimes via a pump to
keep on top of pain. One of the side effects of morphine-based painkillers is constipation and
so to avoid this, we usually prescribe laxatives to keep the bowels regular.

Agitation is also common and we will prescribe medication that can be given in case this occurs.
Regarding the daughter's concerns about the father's suffering and speeding things up, you
need to explain that although there is nothing that can be done to speed things up, one of the
side effects of morphine-based medications is something called secondary effect, which is that
some of the medication that helps with pain control can in turn slow the breathing. Step 5.
Addressing the emotions and offering an empathetic response.
In this case, the daughter is concerned about the prospects of her father's suffering and
certainly for a long period of time. Although you can't offer precise details, explain that when
patients are less rousable and as poorly as her father, we are probably talking in terms of days
to short weeks at the most. Step 6. It's time to wrap up with a strategy or to summarise.
Patients or relatives who have a clear plan for the future are less likely to feel anxious and
uncertain. Before discussing a treatment plan, it is important to ask patients if they are ready at
that time for such a discussion.

I'm just kind of staying in the house a lot, I don't really have any friends or anything. I mean my

certain types of work and as a freelance photographer I guess that can be kind of a problem

Yeah, it was kind of easier when I was at home because I was obviously, I mean my parents and

first noticed the anxiety kicking in when about five or six years ago so you would have been
about 19? Yeah. And what was happening around that time? I guess I'd finished school about a
year before that and I mean I've always been a bit shy at school but it was never ever, like it
didn't really affect things as much as, not at all as much as it has been doing the last few years I
guess.
It just started when like my friends went to university and I don't know, I felt like I was expected
to kind of move out or just do something and then it just kind of escalated from there. I'd just
stop going to parties or I'd just say no to invitations or I don't know, I thought my job would
help because I mean I love it, I really like doing photography but I'm just kind of getting less

What kind of work is the most difficult for you in your job? I guess when I have to kind of be
working with other people, I don't like that. It's like when I'm trying to kind of do an event or
something where there's a lot of people there, not just photographers but actual, you know, if
I'm like taking photos of people that I don't know, I just kind of find myself saying no. I mean I
want to do them but just it's scary so I just don't do it.
So tell me a bit more about what happens then. So let's focus on maybe an invitation to do a job
with, you know, it's going to involve photography with a group of people and you're going to
have social interaction. What kind of thoughts go through your head? I mean I get really hot

just kind of just try and get out of the situation or just focus on something else so that's why I
like doing shots where it's just me and the camera because then I can just put all my attention
on that instead of having to, you know, be with other people.
Okay so it sounds like you have quite a lot of thoughts rushing through your head then at the
point where you get that invitation you think people will look, people will stare, people will think
I'm a weirdo, there's quite a lot about what you think other people will think and how does that

that situation, I just feel like everyone else is fine and they're normal and I'm just the freak who

can focus on that. Like a work situation? Yeah, a time when you were maybe doing a job with

lot of different people and when they told me about the job I thought it would be fine, I thought
it was just going to be a few other photographers but there were actually people in, you know, I

it was, yeah, it was really cool but I find it, found it really hard to try and focus on that because I
was so, I was kind of feeling really anxious and... So it wasn't what you expected? No, it was... So
how long ago was that? That was two weeks ago. Okay, so it's quite recent. Yeah.
So on that particular day, what were the thoughts that you had in your head when you were in
that situation? Just felt really, just really kind of hot, I couldn't really breathe and just felt like I
wanted to just get out and I was kind of trying really, really hard to just focus and just, you
know, like kind of hold the camera and just not think about anything but I just felt like everyone

can tell you're getting kind of anxious even just thinking about that day. Yeah. Okay, so you're
describing quite a lot there to me, so you're saying that you kind of got hot and sweaty, you
said that you held the camera.
Yeah. What was, do you mean you're kind of trying to hide behind it or? I was just trying to
focus on it, I was just thinking if I could just hold it really tightly it would just, I don't know, I'd
kind of just be able to just get through it and just focus. So you're holding the camera very
tightly? Yeah.
And why was that helpful? Because I felt like I was getting really like hot and flushed and I just
thought at least if I can just, I don't know it sounds weird, but I was just trying to keep my
hands still on it because my hands were kind of sweaty and like shaking like loads like and I
could just tell everyone was looking and they could see and I just thought if I just managed to
hold on to it it wouldn't be as noticeable. Okay, so it sounds like you had a lot of thoughts going
through your head. You said that you worried that everyone's looking at you.
What other thoughts were there that were in your mind? Just that I was just stupid and it was
just really, just felt really like kind of like everyone was just going to be staring and just thinking
that I just felt like everyone was looking at me and just they could tell and just thinking oh what
what's she doing and they could tell what I was just really like sweaty and just okay so like that
they could see that yeah okay yeah um so I was trying to wear black so at least kind of tries to
cover it up and just like a lot of layers so they can't tell but I mean my hands like they were so
shaking I was really red and just was just wishing that I just wasn't there. So I mean you've

already described it to me a little bit but if you think about how you looked that day how how
do you say how do you think you looked? I think just really stupid and like I think my face was
really red I could feel it flushing and I knew that I was probably sweating and shaking like my

everyone could definitely see. Okay and what what did you do about how did you try and

anyway but hopefully if I just tried really hard to just focus and look down not try and like not
look at anyone else and just yeah just kind of try and get on with it as best as I could but.
So you avoided looking at people it sounds like you wore black as well in kind of preparation
anyway. Yeah no I always do that even if it's really hot or I wear just loads of layers and just
because otherwise I'll just be really sweaty and like just people would definitely be able to see

celebrate like that we've done it but I just I went home straight away just got in my car and

Okay.

Maybe a glass or two of wine with my dinner. Yeah, and that's for the whole... Is one or two

How would you say that sounds? Yeah, that sounds okay. Good. So we'll go and proceed with

was elevated.

confidence, exceptional intelligence and invincibility.

family. Yvonne was orientated to time, place and person. She appeared to lack insight into her
symptoms being related to a deterioration of her mental health.

There were no positive cardiac findings that I was able to elicit. The only examination finding

examination today.
During your examination, you rolled the patient onto their left, and you re-auscultated at the
apex. Can you explain why you did this? I rolled the patient onto their left side to attempt to
listen to the murmur of mitral stenosis, which is a mid-diastolic murmur, which is often difficult
to auscultate. I also used the bell of the stethoscope as well as the diaphragm, which is useful
at listening for low-frequency murmurs.
Can you explain the relevance of sitting the patient forward? So when sitting a patient forward,
it helps to bring the heart closer to the front of the chest, which helps to aid with auscultating
for the murmur of aortic regurgitation, which is best heard in expiration at the lower left sternal
edge. If this young patient presents with shortness of breath on exertion, can you tell me how
you would investigate him further? So the first thing I would do would be to take a detailed
history assessing the extent of the exertional breathlessness, checking for any chest pain, also
investigating for signs of syncope or presyncope. I would take a detailed family history.
And then following this, I would perform an ECG and an echocardiogram. And depending on
those findings, I might consider performing a 24-hour heart monitor or a cardiac MRI scan. If
these investigations are suggestive of a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, for instance, what
clinical signs may be present in that situation? So it may be that a patient with hypertrophic
cardiomyopathy has no positive clinical signs on examination, but there are two signs which
you can sometimes see.
The first would be an ejection systolic murmur caused by left ventricular outflow tract
obstruction. And the second would be a pansystolic murmur, which is caused by systolic
anterior motion of the mitral valve, which results in mitral regurgitation. What are the causes of
cardiac hypertrophy? So cardiac hypertrophy can be caused by pressure overload in conditions
such as hypertension, aortic stenosis, or people with a subaortic membrane.
It can be caused by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is a genetic condition. And then there
are other causes of cardiac hypertrophy, such as Fabry's disease, amyloidosis, or mitochondrial
disease. How would you treat hypertrophic cardiomyopathy? So I would, first of all, think about
treating patient's symptoms with beta blockers, and then second line with either disopiramide
or a myosin inhibitor such as Mavacantem.
I would assess a patient for their risk of sudden cardiac death, and consider implanting a
defibrillator or ICD. I would assess patient's genetics to aid with familial evaluation. And in
certain cases of severe disease, patients can be referred for septal reduction therapy, which can
be in the form of either a myomectomy or alcohol septal ablation.
Thank you. Thank you. The majority of patients for the PACES examination will obviously have

some clinical signs, but occasionally, as in this case, the examination can be normal.
You must be aware of this and prepare for this eventuality. This can often throw candidates if
they are not aware of this eventuality and can lead to candidates making up clinical signs in a
desperate attempt to find an abnormality. In this situation, you must have confidence in your
own ability.
And if you truly believe there are no obvious clinical abnormal signs, you should be forthright
enough to say so. There are various ways of presenting a normal examination. You could
simply say, my cardiovascular examination is normal.
Or you could be a bit more expansive and say, the patient was comfortable at rest, pulse 70
beats per minute normal. There were no obvious cardiac murmurs or abnormal clinical signs. It
is perfectly okay, and probably more professional, however, to keep your presentation to the
point.
A lot of candidates feel they must take up a lot of time presenting their findings in the hope that
this will give them less time to be asked questions by the examiner. This can, however, lead to
the presentation sounding more like a medical student rather than an MRCP candidate, and can
often give the examiner a feeling that the candidate is over-presenting irrelevant negative
findings. I would therefore suggest you try and be as succinct as possible.

with the patient. Clear instructions should be given to the patient to follow and you should
ensure you maintain patient comfort at all times. If the clinical examination is normal, then the
examiner's questions may be more general, and as in this case, perhaps involve how to
investigate a patient presenting with breathlessness.

apex. Can you explain why you did this? I rolled the patient onto their left side to attempt to
listen to the murmur of mitral stenosis, which is a mid-diastolic murmur, which is often difficult
to auscultate. I also used the bell of the stethoscope as well as the diaphragm, which is useful
at listening for low-frequency murmurs.
Can you explain the relevance of sitting the patient forward? So when sitting a patient forward,
it helps to bring the heart closer to the front of the chest, which helps to aid with auscultating
for the murmur of aortic regurgitation, which is best heard in expiration at the lower left sternal
edge. If this young patient presents with shortness of breath on exertion, can you tell me how
you would investigate him further? So the first thing I would do would be to take a detailed
history assessing the extent of the exertional breathlessness, checking for any chest pain, also
investigating for signs of syncope or presyncope. I would take a detailed family history.
And then following this, I would perform an ECG and an echocardiogram. And depending on
those findings, I might consider performing a 24-hour heart monitor or a cardiac MRI scan. If
these investigations are suggestive of a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, for instance, what
clinical signs may be present in that situation? So it may be that a patient with hypertrophic
cardiomyopathy has no positive clinical signs on examination, but there are two signs which
you can sometimes see.
The first would be an ejection systolic murmur caused by left ventricular outflow tract
obstruction. And the second would be a pansystolic murmur, which is caused by systolic
anterior motion of the mitral valve, which results in mitral regurgitation. What are the causes of
cardiac hypertrophy? So cardiac hypertrophy can be caused by pressure overload in conditions
such as hypertension, aortic stenosis, or people with a subaortic membrane.
It can be caused by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is a genetic condition. And then there
are other causes of cardiac hypertrophy, such as Fabry's disease, amyloidosis, or mitochondrial
disease. How would you treat hypertrophic cardiomyopathy? So I would, first of all, think about
treating patient's symptoms with beta blockers, and then second line with either disopiramide
or a myosin inhibitor such as Mavacantem.

defibrillator or ICD. I would assess patient's genetics to aid with familial evaluation. And in
certain cases of severe disease, patients can be referred for septal reduction therapy, which can
be in the form of either a myomectomy or alcohol septal ablation.

desperate attempt to find an abnormality. In this situation, you must have confidence in your
own ability.

point.

ensure you maintain patient comfort at all times. If the clinical examination is normal, then the
examiner's questions may be more general, and as in this case, perhaps involve how to
investigate a patient presenting with breathlessness.

I'm going to be honest with you, I am not pleased at all with what it is. I heard some of the staff
around the station on the ward talking about me, which is really, really unprofessional, first of
all. You shouldn't be discussing patients.
And not only that, but when I was listening in, they were talking about, oh, you know, he's in,
think he's got a stroke. There's nothing wrong, he's just got a dangle in his arm and all that
stuff. I mean, that, you know, one of them said, what will he be doing next, slurring his speech?
And we're all having a good laugh.
And they were playing Flippin' Hangman at the time as well on the station. We're supposed to
be busy and we're supposed to be professional. And that is not good enough.
Now, listen, I work for the NHS on a stroke unit, right? At another hospital near to this one. If
my staff got heard talking like that, they'd be big trouble. Of course.
Straight in front of HR they'd be for saying things like that. I mean, what kind of example is that
to give other patients as well? It just sounded like, you know, this guy's a joke. And what he says
is not true.
He's not sick. He's just codding. He's having people on.
That kind of thing. It's just rubbish, all of it. It's not good enough.
Of course, of course. I totally appreciate your frustration. And please do let me apologise on
behalf of the department that this happened because it absolutely shouldn't have happened.
Has it happened before? Not that I'm aware of, but... Nobody said anything to you about it. It
shouldn't have happened on this occasion. Well, it's because there's one that was particularly
gobby.
Sure, OK. And it's just got no right to say that kind of stuff at all. I still believe that I've got quite
a serious condition.
And I don't think people are listening. Now, I've heard that from patients for years. Yeah, of
course.
You're just not listening. You're not engaging with me. I am poorly and you're not doing
anything about it.

And to find it happening to an NHS staff. I mean, we're supposed to be like, well, I wouldn't say
a family, but we're supposed to all work together, aren't we? Of course, of course. And I'm really
sorry that this has happened.
And what I can say is, from my perspective, I can make sure I speak to the staff involved, find
out a little bit more about what happened and escalate it accordingly to the nurse in charge
and the consultant, if need be. And of course, you're well within your right to speak to the
patient advice and liaison service and put in a complaint if you'd like to as well. That's obviously
rubbish though, isn't it? It's a service that's available if need be.
So that's... You know, if I start complaining as well about NHS staff, that's going to go on my
record, isn't it? So I don't know exactly how they deal with complaints, but it shouldn't stop you
from... I mean, am I a patient or am I in NHS? You're very much a patient to us at the moment.
So our job, as with any patient, is to get you better. And certainly this type of discourse that you
heard today is not helpful.
I agree with you on that. And we will investigate it accordingly and make sure we do our best to
make sure it doesn't happen again. Yeah, yeah.
I believe you, but I don't believe the systems that you have here. Sure. I don't have any faith in

Sure. And again, I'm not thinking about me. I'm thinking about your patients.
Of course. They hear that stuff. Yeah.
You know, we've got such a bad reputation at the moment. It's so unfair. Yeah.
And then you've got people behaving like that. No wonder we have a bad reputation. No, no,
you're right.
So certainly that type of incident doesn't help with public opinion. It doesn't help patients get
better. And it certainly should be investigated and addressed.
Yeah. Especially... So don't worry, we will look into that. I just also wanted to have a chat with
you about the actual diagnosis and whether there's anything you needed clarification on,
essentially.
Yeah. Well, obviously, because I work on a stroke. Of course, yeah.
You're very familiar with it. I'm very, yeah, with the symptoms. And I was desperately worried
that that's what... Understandably, yeah.
...I was undergoing. And I'm still finding it a little bit difficult to communicate more. So what's
up here to here is not working well.

My brother had a stroke. Right. Sorry to hear that.
Well, I mean, he's in his early 40s. He shouldn't be having a stroke. Yeah, yeah, of course.
And that's what I'm seeing all the time. Understandable, yeah. People getting younger and
younger.
We sort of speculate, is it to do with stress and things like that? And I do work for a lot of hours.
Absolutely, yeah. It's a stressful job, yeah.
Again, the feedback I got was, oh, it's just stress. What, just stress? Yeah, yeah, yeah. So I agree.
So that's not a particularly helpful way of framing it. So what I will say, some positives to take
away from the investigations you've undergone is that the CT head scan and the MRI scans
you've had have been negative. So there aren't any physical changes there to explain the
symptoms.
And that's actually a really good thing because it suggests that you haven't had a big stroke.
And it's something that we can address in other ways. We know you can have many strokes.
Sure. And you can go on in life without even knowing you've had 30 of them. Sure.
I just want to make clear that that's not exactly... It could be a propensity in the family, couldn't
it? Yeah. Really, if my brothers had one. Yeah, that's a completely fair point to raise.
So we can only base things on the best investigations that we've conducted so far, especially CT
heads and MRI scans are helpful. And it's useful to know that your brain actually looks like it's in
very good shape. There's nothing to suggest you've had a stroke.
That being said, we still need an explanation for your symptoms because it's clearly affecting
your day-to-day life and your ability to work. So you mentioned stress, and I wasn't sure if you'd
heard the term a functional disorder before as well, if that's been... Disorder. Well, a functional
neurological condition, basically.
Is that something you've heard of before? Condition's better. Yeah. Sorry, there's just certain
ways in which we word things.
So what we mean by functional, I mean, sometimes people misconstrue there not being a
physical cause with there not being any cause whatsoever and that patients aren't making
things up, but that's not how we should approach such situations. That's not me. I wouldn't
wage people's time.
Not at all, exactly. I mean, you've got plenty of years working on stroke wards. You know what
you're talking about.
So essentially, what functional disorders mean is that instead of there being a physical cause

for your very, very real symptoms, it's actually coming from more a psychological distress,
which you mentioned earlier. You said you have been under quite a lot of stress recently. Yeah,
but that again sounds like I'm just making it up.
It's all in my head. That's not quite the angle I'm taking. So for example, our brain and our
bodies are quite inextricably linked.
The same way you watch a horror film, your heart starts racing, you see something unpleasant,
you feel a bit nauseous. There's lots of ways in which you can, your mind can process
something and then your body physically manifests something else. So that's how I'd explain
functional disorders.
It's not saying that your symptoms aren't real by any means or that you're putting it on, not by
any stretch of the imagination. All it's saying is that there isn't a physical cause and hence we
need to probe a bit further to figure out if there's anything else lifestyle factor wise in terms of
stresses that may have brought this on. And you already sort of alluded to that yourself.
Well, all right, talking professional to professional, I still think people look down. You haven't
used the words mental health and I think that's really good. But there's still a stigma around
seeking counselling and stuff like that.
So what would you do in this position? Sure. So I certainly think that's an approach we need to
take is essentially trying to address the psychological stresses. And I appreciate there has been
stigma around mental health in the past, but it's something that is actually getting better and
better and there's more robust services.
Yeah, there's more robust services available now and I appreciate there can be long wait times
and there's certain things that are a bit out of our control. But our priority right now, both yours
and mine, is to get you better, get your arm better, get you back at work and get you back
doing everything you enjoy. Exactly, exactly.
And I think one approach is referring you to have some therapy, for example, and being
evaluated from a mental health point of view. And it's not something that you should try and
pin any stigma to because it's something that affects a lot of people and it's really important
that we try and be pragmatic the same way that if you broke a leg, you go and see the
appropriate doctor about it. We need to treat these kinds of conditions the same way with the
same sort of pragmatism.
Does that make sense so far? It makes sense. It doesn't explain to me fully what's going on
physically because there is something going on physically. And I've learned from my career that
people will tell you when there's something wrong.
Of course, yeah. They know when there's something properly wrong. Yeah, for certain, for
certain.

And I feel there is something. For certain. And something I'd like to reiterate with the functional
diagnosis is that it's certainly something we arrive upon once we've excluded everything else.
So we do all these blood tests and MRIs and various things that you had done over the last few
days to make sure that we haven't missed something physical. And you've been through quite a
rigorous panel of investigations and we haven't found anything else to explain the symptoms.
Which is good, yeah.
Which is good, yeah, exactly. And now we have a plan in place to actually address the
psychological stresses that may be precipitating this. So what I'm hoping is that once we get
you referred, get you engaging with these services, you might find that everything actually
starts to get better.
So that's the plan that I would recommend. Okay, but just keep me away from Gobby on that
one. I'll do my best.
Honestly. Is that all right? Does that make sense so far? I know that I can tell you're a good
member of staff. There are good members of staff here.
And it's just, you know, you just can't have people out like that letting you down. Of course, no,
no, I understand. I understand.
I'm sorry you have that experience, but at least we've clarified some things here. Is that all
right? Yeah. All right, thank you very much.
Thank you. This was clearly a very angry patient in the setting of an inappropriate situation
where staff were overheard talking about him. An angry patient must be allowed to explain
their anger and listening empathetically is key, which was done very well here.
Taking the patient's concerns seriously is key and giving an explanation of what you are going
to do about it is very important. Apologizing for how this has made the patient feel is perfectly
acceptable. Candidates need to be careful about apologizing completely for certain situations.
And sometimes these scenarios often need navigating carefully. In a lot of scenarios, the
candidate is being given information about a situation that they have not been directly involved
in. And it must be remembered there are always two sides to every story.
The candidate may suggest that an investigation is needed to get to what has happened exactly
and answer some of the difficult questions or accusations that are being raised. An offer of an
internal investigation or a formal complaint to PALS may be appropriate. The explanation of a
possible functional disorder was handled very well.

used to get hurt.
I used to ask people what happened that I got hurt. Which game are you playing? So, finally, I

And I collected information about things. I asked my relatives. There are some people in the

needed to play.

members. More than two or more than two members.

Ayodhya.
Yes, I want people to know about this game, which is good for the society. Why don't we bring it
up? It is possible that we can do something more in this. Right now, I haven't said much about
this game.
But we have to see where we or the Wikipedians take it. I mean, how do we keep it? We have to
see. In comparison to other games, how do you consider this game to be useful for Wikipedia?
As it has no documentation anywhere.
I mean, in any print media, anywhere. We also searched for it in our Google search. So, we

Something that was already existing somewhere. Something that a person from North India

Now we will know that something like this used to happen. In a way, you have done this to
protect your traditional games. Yes, I have done this to protect them.
There are many games in India that are disappearing because of this. People don't know about

Because of which we are forgetting. Because people don't know. Mainly, what is it? Like our

No one in our country knew about cricket. But whether it is e-media or printed media, which

Because of which it can come up. But Wikipedia also works as a media. People will see and

So, why not? This can also come up like cricket. So, do you think that this will be useful for
Wikipedia? It will be useful for Wikipedia. It will be useful for those who use Wikipedia.
It will be useful for everyone. I don't think that knowledge will harm anyone. This is a type of
knowledge that we were missing somewhere.
Now we are getting it. So, if someone wants to take it, it is fine. Otherwise, at least you know
